Cadenat, Scorpaena loppei, is a demersal scorpionfish whose life-history traits have been characterized from field-collected specimens and laboratory observations at controlled thermal conditions. For females, total length at the onset of gonadal maturation is approximately 7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to the first year of benthic residency. In contrast, the ultimate total length attained by adults approaches 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a value derived from length-frequency distributions of the largest individuals encountered in coastal trawl surveys. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting the considerable fecundity characteristic of scorpaenids, which produce numerous small yolk-laden eggs.

Under the thermal regime typical of the species' Mediterranean habitat (15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]), the interval between egg fertilisation and the emergence of the yolk-sac larva spans 18 days [ab = 18 days]. This prolonged embryonic duration, relative to more warm-water congeners, likely reflects the moderating influence of cooler shelf waters on the rate of blastula and gastrula development. Following eclosion, the endotrophic prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days of free-swimming existence. Once the mouth gapes and retinal differentiation enables prey detection, the larva commences exogenous feeding on planktonic copepod nauplii. The pelagic larval phase persists for several weeks before the morphological transformation of metamorphosis triggers settlement into the demersal microhabitat typical of juvenile S. loppei.

Females experience a prolonged growth trajectory before attaining reproductive competence, a pattern consistent with the relatively slow life-history pace of this species. The maximum longevity under natural conditions has been estimated at 8 years [am = 8 years], a figure that aligns with the modest, sustained growth rates observed in recaptured individuals from mark-recapture studies conducted at the established temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. Beyond this age, senescent adults show a decline in somatic condition and a marked reduction in gonadosomatic index, indicative of post-reproductive physiological deterioration. The achievement of such a lifespan suggests that S. loppei allocates resources preferentially to somatic maintenance and tissue repair during early adulthood, deferring heavy reproductive investment until after several years of benthic consolidation.

Reproductive output in S. loppei has been quantified through dissections of gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. Clutch size varies considerably with maternal body size, with larger females producing proportionally more offspring per spawning event; the maximum recorded fecundity reaches 23 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 23 eggs per clutch] at 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C], a figure derived from oocyte counts and corrected for atresia. This translates to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 23 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 23 eggs per day]. Spawning adults deposit between 1 and 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = between 1 and 2 clutches each year], with the peak of reproductive activity occurring during the spring months when zooplankton abundance is highest. This annual reproductive schedule, combined with the substantial per-clutch output, enables the population to sustain recruitment despite the relatively low survival probabilities of pelagic larvae dispersing across the continental shelf.

Long-term growth records from field-validated length-at-age data indicate that the asymptotic adult mass of S. loppei stabilizes at 236 grams [Wwi = 236 grams], a body size that is intermediate among western Mediterranean scorpaenids. This ultimate wet weight is attained after several years of gradual accretion, with the most rapid mass gains occurring during the juvenile fingerling stage. The capacity to reach this mass is contingent upon access to adequate prey resources, primarily small crustaceans and juvenile fish, which sustain the energetic demands of both somatic growth and gonadal recrudescence. Together, the life-history traits of this species—slow growth, delayed maturation, modest asymptotic size, and iteroparous reproduction—define a demographic strategy well suited to the relatively stable but resource-limited benthic environments it occupies.
